screens.title: Interacting with Smart Contracts: ABIs and Bytecode
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn the two artifacts that bridge Solidity source code and your JavaScript frontend: the Application Binary Interface and the bytecode. The ABI is a JSON description that tells web3. js how to encode function calls, decode return values, and interpret events. Bytecode is the low-level, machine-readable instructions the EVM stores and executes when you deploy a contract. Understanding both is essential because the ABI shapes how your dApp talks to a contract, while the bytecode is what actually lives on the chain. We'll also walk through deployment mechanics — how a transaction with empty recipient and the bytecode in its data field creates a new contract account — and then show how to instantiate a web3. eth. Contract object so you can call view functions with call and change state with send. You will see practical Node. js examples you can run against Ganache, learn common mistakes like missing a from address or undersized gas limits, and finish with event listening to inspect emitted logs. By the end you'll be able to deploy locally and connect a small web3. js script to read and update contract state.

Each objective pairs conceptual clarity with a practical milestone that verifies competency. screens.title: What is the ABI (Application Binary Interface)?
screens.narratorSegment: The Application Binary Interface, or ABI, is the formal JSON description a compiler outputs that lists a contract's functions, inputs, outputs, and events. It doesn't contain the executable code. Instead, it serves as a contract's public schema so external tools like web3. js know how to encode a call to a function and how to decode the raw data returned by the EVM. For example, a function signature with a string parameter and a string return will appear in the ABI with its name, a description of inputs and outputs, and its state mutability. This lets web3. js build the exact binary payload required by the EVM's call encoding rules and later parse the returned bytes into JavaScript values. A common misconception is thinking the ABI is executable or contains security logic; it does not. The ABI is only a mapping layer for encoding and decoding. A practical example is a greeting contract: the ABI lists getGreeting as a view function and setGreeting as nonpayable; web3. js uses that to decide whether to call or send and how to shape the data. Key pitfalls include using an ABI that doesn't match the deployed bytecode or forgetting event fields — both lead to decoding errors or missing listeners. Takeaway: the ABI is your dApp's translator for compact binary EVM interactions.

keyIdea.title: ABI is a translator
keyIdea.text: ABI describes how to encode and decode contract calls and events; it is required but not executable code.

content.html:
Core Concept
Application Binary Interface (ABI)
A JSON array describing functions, inputs, outputs, and events.
  • ABI maps function names to argument and return types so web3.js can encode calls correctly.
  • Events in the ABI include indexed and non-indexed fields for efficient log filtering.
  • ABI does not contain executable bytecode; mismatch between ABI and bytecode causes runtime decoding errors.
Analogy
Think of the ABI as a function catalog: it tells you what inputs to provide and how to read the responses.
ABI Example (simplified)
[
  {
    "inputs": [],
    "name": "greeting",
    "outputs": [{ "internalType": "string", "name": "", "type": "string" }],
    "stateMutability": "view",
    "type": "function"
  },
  {
    "inputs": [{ "internalType": "string", "name": "_newGreeting", "type": "string" }],
    "name": "setGreeting",
    "outputs": [],
    "stateMutability": "nonpayable",
    "type": "function"
  }
]
Concrete example
web3.js uses the ABI entry for getGreeting to construct a call and decode the returned UTF-8 string into JavaScript.
Common mistake
Using an ABI that doesn't match the deployed contract leads to wrong decoding or missing functions.
Key Takeaway

The ABI is the contract's interface specification used by web3.js to talk to deployed bytecode.

screens.title: Bytecode and the EVM
screens.narratorSegment: Bytecode is the compiled output of your Solidity contract that the Ethereum Virtual Machine executes. When you compile with the Solidity compiler, it translates high-level constructs into a stream of low-level opcodes and data that together form the contract's bytecode. This is the artifact that actually gets stored on-chain when you deploy; the ABI is separate and only describes the interface. A deployment transaction includes the bytecode in its data field and an empty recipient address; the EVM creates a new account, stores the bytecode at that account's address, and runs the constructor portion of the code. Bytecode is immutable once stored at an address. A common misunderstanding is to assume the bytecode is human readable or that it contains ABI-like metadata usable at runtime — it does not. For practical debugging, local tools such as Ganache will show the transaction that created the contract, its deployed address, and the gas used. When you deploy in scripts, remember to prepend 0x to the bytecode string. Key consequences: you must compile and deploy accurate bytecode; any change in source yields different bytecode and a different deployed address if redeployed. The takeaway: bytecode is the machine program that the chain stores and executes; the ABI is the map that helps external code speak that language.

keyIdea.title: Bytecode is the on-chain program
keyIdea.text: The compiled machine instructions are stored at a contract address and executed by the EVM; this is what deployment writes to the chain.

content.html:
Definition
Contract Bytecode
Low-level instructions generated by the compiler that the EVM executes and stores on-chain.
  • Deployment sends bytecode in a transaction's data field to create a new contract account.
  • The EVM stores and later executes this(bytecode) immutably at the contract address.
  • Bytecode differs across compilations and includes constructor logic executed during deployment.
Practical note
When using deploy scripts, provide the bytecode as a 0x-prefixed hex string and set an adequate gas limit for deployment.
Deployment mechanics
A deploy transaction has an empty to field. The network executes the bytecode, runs the constructor, and assigns an address where the bytecode lives.
Example
In a Node.js deploy script you pass the bytecode to MyContract.deploy({data: myContractBytecode}) and send the transaction from a local Ganache account.
Common mistake
Forgetting to include 0x before the hex bytecode or underestimating gas for deployment causes immediate failure.
Key Takeaway

Bytecode is immutable machine code stored at the contract address and is what the EVM runs.

screens.title: Contract Deployment Process
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying a contract is a multi-step process you should understand end-to-end. First, compile your Solidity source with a compiler such as solc or Remix; compilation produces the ABI and bytecode. Second, prepare a deployment transaction: it has an empty to field and the bytecode in the data payload; you may include constructor arguments encoded into the data as well. Third, submit the transaction from an externally owned account; that transaction must be signed either locally or by a wallet connected to your node. Fourth, miners (or your local Ganache) execute the transaction: the EVM runs the bytecode's initialization code, executes the constructor, and creates a contract account where the code is stored. Fifth, the node returns a receipt that includes the new contract address and gas used. A misconception is that deployment returns a function reference or handle; instead you receive an address and must instantiate a web3. eth. Contract with the ABI and that address to interact. Example: in a Node. js script you call MyContract. deploy({data: myContractBytecode}). send({from: deployer, gas:1500000}), then read deployedContract. options. address from the result. Always check the receipt and Ganache UI to verify gas used and the created address. This step-by-step clarity prevents common deployment errors.

keyIdea.title: Deployment steps
keyIdea.text: Compile → prepare transaction with bytecode → sign and send → EVM executes constructor → contract address and receipt returned.

content.html:
Process Flow
Contract Deployment — step by step
  1. Compile: produce ABI and bytecode with Remix or solc.
  2. Prepare deploy tx: set data to bytecode, include constructor args if needed.
  3. Sign & send: send from an EOA; for local testing use a Ganache account.
  4. EVM execution: runs initialization and stores code at new address.
  5. Receipt: inspect the receipt for contractAddress and gasUsed.
Scenario
When you deploy MyFirstContract locally, Ganache will show a deploy transaction. Use the receipt to instantiate the contract object for subsequent calls and sends.
Checks and tips
  • Always include 0x prefix on bytecode strings in scripts.
  • Provide a gas or gasLimit estimate; underestimates cause failures.
  • Verify constructor args are encoded when present.
  • Confirm the returned contract address and update your front-end configuration.
Key Takeaway

Deployment is a transaction with bytecode that produces a new contract address and a receipt you must inspect.

screens.title: Instantiating web3.eth.Contract
screens.narratorSegment: Once a contract is deployed and you have its address and ABI, the next step is to create a JavaScript representation that lets your app call functions and listen for events. In web3. js you construct a contract object with new web3. eth. Contract(abi, address). The ABI tells web3. js which methods and events exist and how to encode parameters; the address points to the deployed code on the network. That object exposes a. methods property for function calls and. events for subscription to logs. A frequent confusion is where to store the ABI and address: the ABI is static per compiled binary and can be bundled with the front end, while the deployed address is environment-specific — different for local Ganache, testnets, and mainnet. Practically, store the ABI file in your project and configure addresses per network. Example instantiation from the chapter: const myContract = new web3. eth. Contract(myContractABI, contractAddress); After instantiation you can call getGreeting with myContract. methods. getGreeting(). call() or send transactions with myContract. methods. setGreeting(...). send({from, gas}). Misconception check: instantiation does not deploy code; it only creates a local handle to interact with already-deployed bytecode at that address. The key is matching ABI and bytecode version to avoid runtime mismatches.

keyIdea.title: ABI + address = handle
keyIdea.text: web3.eth.Contract ties the interface and deployed code into an object you can call and listen to in JavaScript.

content.html:
Definition
Instantiate web3.eth.Contract
Create a JS contract object using the ABI and address to call, send, and listen.
Example instantiation:
// Example from the chapter
const myContractABI = [ /* ABI array copied from compilation */ ];
const contractAddress = '0xYourDeployedContractAddressHere';
const myContract = new web3.eth.Contract(myContractABI, contractAddress);
Tip
Keep ABI bundled with your frontend and configure addresses per environment to avoid mismatches between local and remote deployments.
What the contract object exposes
  • .methods — call or send contract functions.
  • .events — subscribe to or query emitted events.
  • .options — contains the address you instantiated with.
Concrete scenario
After deployment, use the receipt's contractAddress to instantiate the object and immediately call a view to display initial state.
Key Takeaway

Instantiation creates a local API to an on-chain contract; it does not deploy or change code.

screens.title: Read-only calls with .call() vs State changes with .send()
screens.narratorSegment: Web3. js exposes two primary interaction patterns with contract functions:. call() for read-only operations and. send() for state-changing transactions. A. call() is used with functions marked view or pure in Solidity. It executes locally on your connected node, does not create a transaction on-chain, and therefore costs no gas. Use call when you just need to fetch values, like reading a public counter or getGreeting. In contrast,. send() submits a transaction that modifies contract state. It must be signed by an externally owned account and consumes gas paid by the sender. When calling. send() you need to include a from address and often a gas or gasLimit parameter. The network creates an on-chain transaction, miners execute it, and the operation appears in the chain and transaction receipts. A common misconception: that. call() is safer because it doesn't alter state — true — but a read obtained via call might be outdated if a transaction has not yet been mined. In practice you will combine both: use. call() to display current state and. send() to request a state update. After. send() completes, verify the updated value with another. call() and inspect the transaction receipt for gas used and event logs. Misconfiguring from or gas will lead to failures; always test on a local chain like Ganache first.

keyIdea.title: call() vs send()
keyIdea.text: call() is free and local for view/pure functions; send() submits signed transactions that change state and cost gas.

content.html:
Comparison
call() vs send()
.call()
  • For view/pure functions; executes locally.
  • No transaction is created and no gas cost.
  • Good for reads or UI display values.
const currentGreeting = await myContract.methods.getGreeting().call();
console.log(currentGreeting);
.send()
  • For nonpayable/payable functions that change state.
  • Requires a signed transaction, a from address, and gas.
  • Produces a transaction receipt and may emit events.
const receipt = await myContract.methods.setGreeting("Hello").send({
  from: deployerAccount,
  gas: 100000
});
console.log(receipt.gasUsed);
Example
Read the greeting with call, then update with send, then verify with call again.
Misconception
Calling a view function with call will not reflect unmined transactions; always check receipts for finality.
Key Takeaway

Use call for cheap reads; use send when you want to change state and accept gas costs and signatures.

screens.title: Node.js Script: Deploy and Interact (interactContract.js)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the provided Node. js script that connects to a local Ganache instance, deploys a contract, reads state, sends a transaction to update state, and listens for an event. The script starts by creating a Web3 instance pointed at Ganache's RPC URL. Next it defines the ABI and the bytecode copied from the Remix compile output. For deployment, it creates a new contract object with new web3. eth. Contract(myContractABI) and calls deploy with the bytecode and constructor args. The send step requires a from address and gas parameter. After deployment the script captures deployedContract. options. address and re-initializes a contract handle with that address to perform interactions. It reads the initial greeting using. call(), then uses. send() to change the greeting and awaits the transaction receipt. The script also sets up an event listener for GreetingUpdated by calling myDeployedContract. events. GreetingUpdated with a fromBlock filter. A useful debugging step is to log receipt. blockNumber and gasUsed. Common mistakes include forgetting to replace the placeholder bytecode or not passing the deployer's account as from, which results in a failed send. This walkthrough clarifies the role of each block in the script and what to inspect in Ganache when you run it.

Code Walkthrough
interactContract.js — key sections
Setup and ABI/Bytecode
const Web3 = require('web3');
const ganacheRpcUrl = 'http://127.0.0.1:7545';
const web3 = new Web3(ganacheRpcUrl);
// Paste ABI and bytecode from Remix here
Note: The ABI is a JSON array; bytecode must be 0x-prefixed hex.
Deploy, interact, and events
// Deploy
const MyContract = new web3.eth.Contract(myContractABI);
const deployedContract = await MyContract.deploy({ data: myContractBytecode }).send({ from: deployerAccount, gas: 1500000 });

// Instantiate with address
const myDeployedContract = new web3.eth.Contract(myContractABI, deployedContract.options.address);

// Call
const currentGreeting = await myDeployedContract.methods.getGreeting().call();

// Send
const receipt = await myDeployedContract.methods.setGreeting("Hello from Web3.js!").send({ from: deployerAccount, gas: 100000 });

// Events
myDeployedContract.events.GreetingUpdated({ fromBlock: receipt.blockNumber }).on('data', event => { /* ... */ });
Run checklist
Start Ganache, paste your ABI and bytecode, replace addresses, then run node interactContract.js.
Debug tip
If send fails, check the from address, unlock the account or configure the provider to sign transactions, and increase gas limit.
Key Takeaway

The script ties together compile artifacts and local infrastructure; inspect receipts and Ganache to confirm correct execution.

screens.title: Event Listening and Log Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Events are how contracts emit structured logs that external applications can subscribe to or query. When a contract emits an event, the EVM stores it in the transaction receipt logs. The ABI lists events with input definitions and indexed fields; indexed fields allow efficient filtering by topics. In web3. js you can listen for events using myContract. events. EventName({ fromBlock }) and register a data handler that receives decoded return values. In the example, GreetingUpdated includes oldGreeting, newGreeting, and updater; the listener gives you event. returnValues with those fields ready to examine. A practical pattern is to listen starting from the transaction's block number to capture events produced by the transaction you just sent. Misconceptions include assuming events are a source of truth for state — events are logs and can be pruned in some environments; always verify state via a call if you need canonical data. Another pitfall is forgetting to include the ABI event entry; without it web3. js cannot decode the log. Use event listeners to update UI reactively or log activity in your backend. In local testing with Ganache, events are typically instantaneous and visible in the transaction details; use receipts to correlate events and gas usage.

keyIdea.title: Events are decoded logs
keyIdea.text: Use the ABI to decode event logs; listen from an appropriate block to capture relevant events and update your UI or logs.

content.html:
Process Flow
Event Listening & Log Handling
Listen pattern
myDeployedContract.events.GreetingUpdated({
  fromBlock: receipt.blockNumber
}).on('data', event => {
  console.log('Old:', event.returnValues.oldGreeting);
  console.log('New:', event.returnValues.newGreeting);
});
Start listening from the block containing the transaction to ensure you capture that event.
Event decoding
The ABI entry for the event must match the emitted event fields for web3.js to decode returnValues successfully. Indexed fields become topics available for filtering.
Common mistake
Not including the event in the ABI or using the wrong ABI version prevents decoding; you'll receive raw logs instead of structured returnValues.
Use case
Update a UI when a greeting changes by listening for GreetingUpdated and refreshing displayed state.
Best practice
Correlate events with contract state via a subsequent call if you need authoritative data.
Key Takeaway

Events provide useful signals decoded via the ABI; use them for reactive UI updates but confirm state with calls when needed.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging Tips
screens.narratorSegment: When interacting with contracts you'll encounter a handful of repeatable errors. The most frequent are: missing or incorrect from address on. send(), insufficient gas or gas limit too low, ABI mismatch, and using stale contract addresses. To debug, first check the error returned by web3. js and the transaction receipt if the transaction was submitted. Receipts include gasUsed and status; a status of zero indicates failure. In Ganache, inspect the transaction list and click into the failing transaction to view revert messages and gas consumed. Another tip is to enable verbose logging in your provider or inspect the node's transaction pool. For ABI mismatches you may see functions undefined or decoding errors — always copy the ABI produced by the same compilation used to produce the bytecode you deployed. When using wallets like MetaMask, ensure the selected account matches your from address or that the provider will sign the transaction. For constructor mistakes, verify constructor arguments are encoded correctly in the deploy data. A concrete debugging flow: reproduce the failure on Ganache, run the same send with console logs around the gas and from fields, check the receipt for status and gasUsed, and then correct the script. These steps will help you quickly identify and fix the typical interaction issues.

keyIdea.title: Debug systematically
keyIdea.text: Inspect receipts, Ganache UI, and ABI versions; confirm from address and gas settings to resolve common failures.

content.html:
Troubleshooting
Why transactions fail and how to debug
Checklist for failures
  • Confirm the from address is correct and unlocked in your provider.
  • Increase gas limit if you hit out-of-gas errors.
  • Verify ABI and deployed bytecode come from the same compilation.
  • Check receipt.status; zero means revert.
Using Ganache and receipts
Ganache shows transactions with gas used and revert traces. Use the transaction receipt in your script to examine gasUsed, blockNumber, and logs for emitted events.
Example fix
If a .send() fails due to gas, increase the gas value in the send call, re-run on Ganache, and confirm the receipt shows status true and updated state.
Developer habit
Log values before sending, then inspect the receipt and Ganache UI to match console outputs with chain events.
Misconception
Assuming a thrown error always means the contract code is wrong; often it's a configuration or gas issue in the client code.
Key Takeaway

Diagnose by checking receipts, Ganache traces, ABI versions, and from/gas settings; fix the client configuration first.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts you need to carry forward. Keep these three concepts clear: ABI for interface, bytecode for machine code, and deployment for creating the contract account. Use these ideas when building your front end and scripts to avoid mismatches and runtime errors. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn the two artifacts that bridge Solidity source code and your JavaScript frontend: the Application Binary Interface and the bytecode. The ABI is a JSON description that tells web3. js how to encode function calls, decode return values, and interpret events. Bytecode is the low-level, machine-readable instructions the EVM stores and executes when you deploy a contract. Understanding both is essential because the ABI shapes how your dApp talks to a contract, while the bytecode is what actually lives on the chain. We'll also walk through deployment mechanics — how a transaction with empty recipient and the bytecode in its data field creates a new contract account — and then show how to instantiate a web3. eth. Contract object so you can call view functions with call and change state with send. You will see practical Node. js examples you can run against Ganache, learn common mistakes like missing a from address or undersized gas limits, and finish with event listening to inspect emitted logs. By the end you'll be able to deploy locally and connect a small web3. js script to read and update contract state.

These objectives guide the practical skills you'll gain. First, you'll explain the ABI: what the JSON includes and why web3. js needs it to encode arguments, decode return values, and map event logs to structured data. Second, you'll describe bytecode: how the Solidity compiler produces the machine instructions that the EVM executes and why bytecode is what gets stored at a contract address. Third, you'll understand contract deployment mechanics: what a deployment transaction looks like, why the to field is empty, and how constructor execution and address assignment work during deployment. Fourth, you'll instantiate a web3. eth. Contract object using a contract's ABI and deployed address so it becomes a live JavaScript representation you can call and send to. Each objective pairs conceptual clarity with a practical milestone that verifies competency. We'll include simple mnemonics or tiny visual cues so you remember which artifact does what, and a verification step you can run locally with Ganache to confirm each objective.

These objectives focus on hands-on actions you'll perform. First, you'll use web3. js. call() to read view or pure functions, learning why these operations do not cost gas and execute locally on your node. Second, you'll use web3. js. send() to submit state-changing transactions, including how to provide a from address and a gas limit, and how signing and gas consumption work. Third, you'll learn to listen for contract events emitted from functions so you can react to on-chain changes in your application and inspect event return values. Fourth, you'll practice deploying to a local Ganache chain and verifying the deployment address and transaction receipt in the Ganache UI. Each card includes a short verification step and a visual mnemonic to help you remember the right method to use for read versus write operations. These skills let you complete the hands-on activity: deploy MyFirstContract locally, read its greeting, update it, and observe the emitted GreetingUpdated event.

The Application Binary Interface, or ABI, is the formal JSON description a compiler outputs that lists a contract's functions, inputs, outputs, and events. It doesn't contain the executable code. Instead, it serves as a contract's public schema so external tools like web3. js know how to encode a call to a function and how to decode the raw data returned by the EVM. For example, a function signature with a string parameter and a string return will appear in the ABI with its name, a description of inputs and outputs, and its state mutability. This lets web3. js build the exact binary payload required by the EVM's call encoding rules and later parse the returned bytes into JavaScript values. A common misconception is thinking the ABI is executable or contains security logic; it does not. The ABI is only a mapping layer for encoding and decoding. A practical example is a greeting contract: the ABI lists getGreeting as a view function and setGreeting as nonpayable; web3. js uses that to decide whether to call or send and how to shape the data. Key pitfalls include using an ABI that doesn't match the deployed bytecode or forgetting event fields — both lead to decoding errors or missing listeners. Takeaway: the ABI is your dApp's translator for compact binary EVM interactions.

Bytecode is the compiled output of your Solidity contract that the Ethereum Virtual Machine executes. When you compile with the Solidity compiler, it translates high-level constructs into a stream of low-level opcodes and data that together form the contract's bytecode. This is the artifact that actually gets stored on-chain when you deploy; the ABI is separate and only describes the interface. A deployment transaction includes the bytecode in its data field and an empty recipient address; the EVM creates a new account, stores the bytecode at that account's address, and runs the constructor portion of the code. Bytecode is immutable once stored at an address. A common misunderstanding is to assume the bytecode is human readable or that it contains ABI-like metadata usable at runtime — it does not. For practical debugging, local tools such as Ganache will show the transaction that created the contract, its deployed address, and the gas used. When you deploy in scripts, remember to prepend 0x to the bytecode string. Key consequences: you must compile and deploy accurate bytecode; any change in source yields different bytecode and a different deployed address if redeployed. The takeaway: bytecode is the machine program that the chain stores and executes; the ABI is the map that helps external code speak that language.

Deploying a contract is a multi-step process you should understand end-to-end. First, compile your Solidity source with a compiler such as solc or Remix; compilation produces the ABI and bytecode. Second, prepare a deployment transaction: it has an empty to field and the bytecode in the data payload; you may include constructor arguments encoded into the data as well. Third, submit the transaction from an externally owned account; that transaction must be signed either locally or by a wallet connected to your node. Fourth, miners (or your local Ganache) execute the transaction: the EVM runs the bytecode's initialization code, executes the constructor, and creates a contract account where the code is stored. Fifth, the node returns a receipt that includes the new contract address and gas used. A misconception is that deployment returns a function reference or handle; instead you receive an address and must instantiate a web3. eth. Contract with the ABI and that address to interact. Example: in a Node. js script you call MyContract. deploy({data: myContractBytecode}). send({from: deployer, gas:1500000}), then read deployedContract. options. address from the result. Always check the receipt and Ganache UI to verify gas used and the created address. This step-by-step clarity prevents common deployment errors.

Once a contract is deployed and you have its address and ABI, the next step is to create a JavaScript representation that lets your app call functions and listen for events. In web3. js you construct a contract object with new web3. eth. Contract(abi, address). The ABI tells web3. js which methods and events exist and how to encode parameters; the address points to the deployed code on the network. That object exposes a. methods property for function calls and. events for subscription to logs. A frequent confusion is where to store the ABI and address: the ABI is static per compiled binary and can be bundled with the front end, while the deployed address is environment-specific — different for local Ganache, testnets, and mainnet. Practically, store the ABI file in your project and configure addresses per network. Example instantiation from the chapter: const myContract = new web3. eth. Contract(myContractABI, contractAddress); After instantiation you can call getGreeting with myContract. methods. getGreeting(). call() or send transactions with myContract. methods. setGreeting(...). send({from, gas}). Misconception check: instantiation does not deploy code; it only creates a local handle to interact with already-deployed bytecode at that address. The key is matching ABI and bytecode version to avoid runtime mismatches.

Web3. js exposes two primary interaction patterns with contract functions:. call() for read-only operations and. send() for state-changing transactions. A. call() is used with functions marked view or pure in Solidity. It executes locally on your connected node, does not create a transaction on-chain, and therefore costs no gas. Use call when you just need to fetch values, like reading a public counter or getGreeting. In contrast,. send() submits a transaction that modifies contract state. It must be signed by an externally owned account and consumes gas paid by the sender. When calling. send() you need to include a from address and often a gas or gasLimit parameter. The network creates an on-chain transaction, miners execute it, and the operation appears in the chain and transaction receipts. A common misconception: that. call() is safer because it doesn't alter state — true — but a read obtained via call might be outdated if a transaction has not yet been mined. In practice you will combine both: use. call() to display current state and. send() to request a state update. After. send() completes, verify the updated value with another. call() and inspect the transaction receipt for gas used and event logs. Misconfiguring from or gas will lead to failures; always test on a local chain like Ganache first.

The script starts by creating a Web3 instance pointed at Ganache's RPC URL. Next it defines the ABI and the bytecode copied from the Remix compile output.
